title: What is your process?
author: Officialpolygrafix
selftext:
Hey folks, just curious what your process is like to develop your game?  
I'm  a game developer of 24 years who has worked at studios large and small, and currently solo deving on a unique business management sim.   
I've developed what i think is a really good process, that mirrors how it works in a studio using a combination of waterfall and agile production methods. Goes something like this:  
1. setup claude + mcp + unity, environment and repo  
2. create a game design document (GDD), then feed that into the LLM side of the AI. Have it poke holes in the design, work with it to flush out any shortcomings.  
3. Build a production map timeline, organize the game by groups of tasks (mini-milestones)  
4. Have the LLM side write the prompt to send over to the code side (also claude, claude code in my case), to execute on that group of tasks and write a report when it's done. Note: Each mini-milestone(group of tasks) gets it's own session, to keep context length short and on point for that specific milestone.  
5. When it finishes, take the report back to the LLM side for review where we discuss what code did, what it didn't do, where it fits on the big picture, any thing i may need to be aware of before playtesting.  
6. Playtest the game. Take my own notes and suggestions.  
7. Feed my playstest notes back into the LLM, Corraberate with it, and then it prompts the next task it had planned, but also figures out where to add in my suggestions and bug reports from the playest i just did.  
8. Repeat this process from step 4.

I've pretty much got through most of my game doing this, and it's turning out great. Was curious how you all are building your games?

comments.author: RUSuper
comments.body:
1) Setup MCP  
2) Setup .md files and tell Claude which .md files to write during process  
2) Make core loop of the game (Which probably changes anyway)  
3) Make starting area   
4) Make basic HUD  
5) Make in game editors for editing things like HUD and position of objects by myself instead of endlessly asking Claude to do it for me  
6) Get bunch more ideas  
7) Think about "Ok this might be too many ideas abort the mission"  
8) Polish what I have  
9) Once enough systems are in game dedicate one session for one system and "manager" session (HUD session,Graphic session etc)  
10) Polish again  
11) Roleplay game publishing company by roleplaying CEO while each session is one team - works surprisingly well since alternative is to read 50 different sessions, this way one "main" session sends messages to other sessions and I don't have to keep an eye on 50 different sessions (rarely)

That would be it

replies.author: Officialpolygrafix
replies.body:
For me, I'm already a veteran 3d artist of 26 years, so im doing my own modeling. I use 3d studio max because thats what i learned on. however, i'm hearing great things about using blender with mcp to create 3d models.   That may be a good alternative for getting 3d assets into your game.   
There's also Tripo ai and meshy 3d, which are online platforms which allows you to generate 3d models from prompts. I've played around with them, and they seem pretty good, although i'd question whether they would animate well as is.  I think if it's just basic props, then these ai solutions are probably pretty descent, but for more intricate character work where they will animate well, im not sure, i havent progressed that far with it, but i know the are working towards a solution for this and i tried those programs probably a year ago so maybe they've already figured it out. Anyway, thats some good options if you dont know blender that well.

comments.author: cckynv
comments.body:
Seems pretty similar to my own workflow:

1. UnityMCP + OMP harness

2. Game Design Document -> turned into playbook for each development phase (broken down into manageable phases with deliverables and milestones)
3. Ingest CLAUDE.md - contains hard rules, documentation requirement (CHANGELOG.md), design decisions, execution guidelines (automate what is automate-able, handoff whatever can't)

4. Ingest CHANGELOG.md - living record of changes, edits, and decisions. Updated by the AI after every batch of changes

5. Ingest PLAYBOOK-STEP-#.md - detailed playbook that the AI follows. Contains requirements, pass/fail criteria, smoke testing steps, etc.

6. Direct the AI to start wherever it left off on the playbook based on the changelog record.

7. Let it work, handle whatever it flags for me to handle.

8. Playtest once it finishes a batch of changes. Record bugs or necessary changes in ITERATION.md

9. Ingest ITERATION.md, then repeat from step 6.

comments.author: heavy-minium
comments.body:
I‘m still trialing the method, but right now I‘m attempting a „working backward“ method. I basically produced a full game wiki that is exhaustive, linked, and with AI generated images.  As well as fictional player testimonials about the game - all as if it would already exists.

The instructions are to l continuously work on the next full vertical - which basically means to fully implement what is described on a page on a defined set of dimensions (controls/rendering/audio/serialization/etc). So the work is basically page by page and links between pages are followed to dependent pages. Progress on verticals is tracked in a file. AI agents usually make suffiencitly good decisions about what the next vertical should be, the interlinked pages help understanding the chain of dependencies.

I’m still the loop for most assets which ain’t AI-generated but partially bought and hand-crafted.

So far the results are promising. This obviously only works if you exactly know what the full game is to be. Works in my case because it’s easy to imagine upfront, I’m heavily leaning into existing farming sims, and I was looking into existing game wikis to take note of the kind of content I should write down. It was a lot of work, though, but now things are basically on autopilot. And even if it doesn’t work out, the wiki has lots of value for trying again later with more powerful models, or even normal development.

comments.author: butchiebags
comments.body:
I am building a game in unreal 5.8, but it’s gotten further and further away from unreal and into its own process that piggybacks on the engine.  I basically just built the editor into the game, probably not too different from what you have.  

This is my first time seriously attempting a game but I’ve been a C# dotnet dev for the past 10 years professionally.

Here’s the layout:

1. Many specs organized by domain and feature (pretty messy, could be better)  
2. Handoff.md that tracks current work and an index for planned work  
3. Bugs.md which is appended from my own chat commands in the game, so as I playtest I can just /bug and it drops the message with location data etc.  I also have a /feature which basically works the same.  The handoff has instructions for an orchestrator to triage bugs and features into bigger tasks that worktree agents can take  
4. CLI for agents to do repro, so teleport around the game, move, generate items, etc.  
5. Gigantic debug menu in the game with like 300 knobs and sliders right now to tune everything so I don’t have to mess with code  
6. Rulings.md for any decisions I need to make like clarifications on features, post-playtest review, the orchestrator walks through all of these when I want to revisit things.

It feels pretty good to me, doesn’t get too overwhelming and I can focus on what I want when I want without to much churn.  I’ve been working on it for about 3 months very consistently and I spend a majority of my Claude 5x plan on it, able to get through about 2 runs every day with about 4-5 agents working concurrently.  I use fable as an orchestrator and opus 5 for coding agents.  My focus to this point has been all the systems and I’m just wrapping up the graphics and lighting with a lot of unique stuff going on.  I’ve built agent skills for working with assets, an in-game DAW for wavetable synthesis for sfx and music, and the skills are designed to let me add and edit assets/music/sfx and I want to use qwen 3.8 for some of the long running workflows.

comments.author: IcyBother8850
comments.body:
Code pipeline:

1. Design doc

2. Development stages doc.

3. Each dev stage split into actionable tasks docs

4. Prompt gpt task by task, test and bugfix where appropriate.

Stuff I develop in parallel following the same workflow as the need arises:

1. Map Editor

2. UI Editor

Assets pipeline:

1. GPT creates concept art with empty background .png

2. Meshy creates the models from them with textures + animations

3. Normalize models in blender + add extra weapon sockets etc...

4. Import models ingame test and accept or fix again in blender

comments.author: brawnyai_redux
comments.body:
I use Codex instead Cladue. The GPT SOL 5.6 is pretty good in general, might not create graphics as nice as Claude but gameplay and other things are solid.

1. I use ChatGPT SOL Pro to save token from my Codex and I asked to research about the games that overlaps or share things I want to create on my own.  
2. Then, I asked it to write a prompt to create the game design and implementation definitions and prompt tuned for GPT SOL 5.6  
3. I paste the prompt into Codex SOL 5.6 Extra High with Plan mode on.  
4. It will ask me clarifying questions  
5. I answered them as much as I can and if I don't like any response, I type my own.  
6. Once the plan is created, I give permission to implement.   
7. Once the game is done, I play and keep the back and forth cycles of improvements.  
8. I think later is more important. Creating the game that is playable by LLM, so the agents can play and discover how to balance the game better and find out other dynamics to improve the game mechanics, balance the game, and find dynamics that may not be good for gameplay.  
9. Then it cycle through the feedback time.   
10. Also build the game where the graphic and visual elements can be changed easily, so you have the game engine with the rules, independent from the graphic side of it. So I can keep improving the game play without worrying about the image/3d/2d/visual side. That can be improved separately.   
11. All games are created in vanilla html, css, js (only import js libraries that is harder to replicate such as three.js, but otherwise avoid using third party tools for maximum compatibility)

replies.author: Officialpolygrafix
replies.body:
Solid production method.  
I've used codex in the past, the same way on another game i started but haven't finished yet. Once i get done with teh game i'm working on i'll get back to that

comments.author: C0L0SSUSvdm
comments.body:
$20 claude subscription, blender mcp, and Godot. 

I ask it to decide its own milestones, and to keep the context window low i start a new chat/conversation for each milestone. I use the gauntlet loop, but i specify i only want it looped for the milestone we're at in the current conversation. At the end, i have it review and check everything as a whole with the same loop review process.


My goal is to get it as close to shippable before i start doing my own work on the project myself to bring it closer to perfect. My experience is in design, not at all a programmer really. Cant grasp patterns and architecture.

replies.author: Officialpolygrafix
replies.body: thats the solution right there. Keep each task (or small group of tasks) in it's own thread, so you don't reach context limits and drift.  I do this with the code side.. But for the LLM side i chat with about the game, I want it to have the full context and keep those sessions long, although i've had to break them down into 6 seperate sessions due to reaching limits, it writes the important things to an md file it can access to context when i have to start a new llm session.

replies.author: C0L0SSUSvdm
replies.body:
One mistake i had to make to relize is that claude chat and claude code do not share info. 


I had in the beginning got claude chat to write my .md files for me, only for claude code to build errors from it. "Oh i got this error because the .md told me not to do w/e"

replies.author: Officialpolygrafix
replies.body:
yep, you become the bridge between them. Thats exactly what i do. I use the chat/llm side to orchestrate and have discussion about the project, and it writes the prompts for the tasks i manually send over to code. Would be great if these two talked.

Sometimes i catch parts of the conversation like "Designer was doing work in 3ds studio max while i was trying to work in unity. I tried 3d times and failed" or "Designer was changing things around in unity while i was trying to work, please ask designer to stay out of unity during this time"  
I'm paraphrasing, but it's logged in some of my task reports. Lol
